content.text:
From the critic's visit you asked for:

**Critic's notes, fourth visit**

**What you asked about**

*The sides of the falls.* Yes, they read as water now. On the left the dark wedges open as gaps between strands. The few white threads all differ, and the sheet frays from about y 720 down while the top stays coherent. That's how a fall behaves. At full view the curtain widens as it drops, and in squint it no longer has a drawn outline. The right side is nearly there, but one spot is still too regular. Between x 615–640 and y 790–850 there are four or five threads, all at the same slant, about the same length and evenly spaced. Up close they look like a rake. At full view they soften into spray, but the even spacing still shows. Below them, three small white tongues point down over the right foot rock (x ~622–634, y 850–870) and read as teeth. If those marks are still wet, lift one or two threads from the middle of the fan with a 12-wide dipped rag, so the gaps are uneven and one thread stays longer than the rest. Lift two of the three tongues. That takes a few minutes.

*The trunk at x ~255–268.* It reads as a far trunk coming out of the foliage and fading into the haze. Accept it. If you go back in while it's open, warm the top 60 units slightly. It's a little bluer than anything else in the haze, which makes it a touch more noticeable than it should be. That's optional.

*Your two open passages.* I agree with accepting both. The stream reads as a far water surface at full view, and the foam reads as foam drifting on water.

**What I'd take up first: the foreground rock, lower left (x 0–310, y 1055–1250)**

It's the nearest thing in the picture and the largest single dark shape. Right now it's also the most formula-like. You have a smooth dome with an olive band the same width all the way around it, following the contour exactly, from the top at the left down the steep right side to the frame at x ~300. That's the even horseshoe from your scratch trial 3. The orange leaves along it are spaced like beads, at about (60,1068), (175,1082) and (232,1105). The edges view shows why it reads as a drawn ring. The rock's outline against the water is nearly lost, because the two are close in value, so the only hard line is the inner edge of the band, running parallel to the outline. It also repeats the dark-loaf-with-even-green-cap shape of the three mid-ground loaves, here at the biggest size. You accepted those loaves for good reasons, and fixing this rock breaks the repetition without touching them.

Do it with a few large planes. No cracks or small single marks; you've already learned what those do here.

- The light comes from the glow behind and above, so only surfaces that face up would catch it. Keep the moss on the flatter top (x 0 to about 200) as an area rather than a band. Let its lower edge wander: wider at the left, around 35 units, narrowing and stopping around x 240–250, y ~1115.
- On the steep right side, from about y 1115 to the bottom, cover the band with rock body dark (lent/rock) so that side turns into shadow and merges with the water's value at its edge.
- Run a thin, broken warm rim along the top edge of the silhouette with the knife held along the edge, only where it faces the glow (x ~110–240). The outline is then clear there and lost everywhere else.
- Keep two leaves close together and drop the rest, so they read as fallen leaves rather than a pattern.
- Optional second step: let the top run flatter out to about x 230 and turn down at a corner, rather than following one continuous arc. Add rock dark over the flat water at the shoulder (x 200–260, y 1075–1110). Dark over a plain mid-gray won't leave a patch that looks stuck on.

All of this goes over dry paint, so if it fails it lifts clean.

**Lesser item, only if it's cheap**

The white ripple marks across the dark water on the left (x 20–330, y 930–1060) are all the same weight, all straight, and scattered evenly. They're the hardest marks in the lower third. If you can quiet three or four in the middle of the dark area without leaving patches, the remaining ones near the light column will look more like glints. If you can't, leave them. They're dry, and covering them could cause more harm than they do now.

After the rock and the right threads, I'd call it finished. The light runs from the glow to the falls to the foam to the pool without a break, and the falls now read as falling water.

content.thinking:
I'm analyzing the fgRock2 mask's silhouette contours to find the top and right edges per coordinate, then planning to cover the olive band along the steep right side with the darker rock body color by computing the band as the mask minus a shrunken version of itself.

Checking the expected gray values: rock body dark around 50, water nearby around 95, so clipping the dark body to fgRock2 would create a crisp dark edge against the water, unlike the current olive band which blends more smoothly. I'm weighing whether to keep that hard edge as an intentional shadow silhouette or soften it to merge better with the water tone.

For the mossy flat top, I want to redefine the lower boundary as a wandering curve that's wider on the left and tapers off near x=240, instead of the uniform band currently there — then repaint areas that fall outside this new boundary as either rock-dark or moss accordingly, with a graded transition at the seam similar to the earlier mossdeep-to-rock fix.

Simpler approach: repaint the whole upper zone as a single pass with graded piling — moss tones near the top blending down into rock/lichen tones below the new wandering boundary line, using the flat-7 technique oriented along the surface contour, clipped to the rock shape, with a soft blend layered on top for natural, irregular edges.

Next I want to vary the width of that band with x, add a warm broken rim of knife strokes along the top edge facing the glow (around x 110–240, using light pressure and load with the blade oriented along the contour), and thin out the leaf cluster down to just two — keeping the ones near canvas coordinates (62,1071) and (174,1082), dropping the third one near (232,1106).

I want to flatten the top contour out to about x=230 and then turn down at a corner, with rock dark added over the water near the shoulder. Mapping the current top line's y-values across x gives a rough curve, so I'm redrawing it flatter from x=200 to x=230 before dropping steeply to rejoin the existing edge around x=280, y=1150.

This breaks up the domed, loaf-like repetition in the rock shape. I'll build a new mask combining the original rock with this added shoulder piece, then repaint the upper zone — starting by nailing down the actual contour numbers.

I addressed the critic's feedback by darkening one thread in the right fan and removing the tongue cover, which restored the original white tongue. Next, I'll measure the contour of the foreground rock.

content.thinking:
I need to adjust the silhouette's top curve, flattening it out before the corner by modifying the control points of fgTop2 to create a smoother transition around x=230.

function poolPiles()
  local function dB(x, y)
    local dx = math.abs(x - 486)
    if dx < 140 then return 0 end
    local len = 45 + 35 * nb:at01(x, 0) + 15 * nb(x * 3, 7)
    return clamp((WL + len * clamp((dx - 140)/30, 0, 1) - y) / 14, 0, 1)
  end
  local function C(x,y) return columnM:at(x,y) end
  local function Wd(x,y) return wedgeM:at(x,y) end
  local function LR(x,y) return math.max(reflL:at(x,y), reflR:at(x,y)) end
  local function B(x,y) return math.max(birchRA:at(x,y), birchRB:at(x,y)) end
  local function rest(x,y) return clamp(1 - C(x,y) - Wd(x,y) - LR(x,y) - B(x,y), 0, 1) end
  return {{lent, function(x,y) return dB(x,y) * 0.5 end},
         {waterdark, function(x,y) return dB(x,y) + rest(x,y) * (1 - dB(x,y)) * 0.35 + C(x,y) * 0.35 * clamp((0.4 - ns:at01(x,y))*3, 0, 1) end},
         {poolmid, function(x,y) return rest(x,y) * (1 - dB(x,y)) end},
         {colmid, function(x,y) return C(x,y) * (1 - Wd(x,y)) * (1 - dB(x,y)) end},
         {foamsh, function(x,y) return C(x,y) * clamp(1 - (y - WL)/60, 0, 1) * (0.5 + 0.5*ns:at01(x,y)) end},
         {glow, function(x,y) return Wd(x,y) * clamp(0.9 - 0.6*math.abs(x - 500)/150, 0, 1) end},
         {amber, function(x,y) return Wd(x,y) * 0.7 + LR(x,y) * 0.15 end},
         {haze, function(x,y) return Wd(x,y) * 0.3 + B(x,y) * 0.7 end},
         {birch, function(x,y) return B(x,y) * 0.35 end},
         {leafshade, function(x,y) return LR(x,y) * (1 - B(x,y)) * 0.8 end},
         {orangeleaf, function(x,y) return LR(x,y) * (1 - B(x,y)) * 0.4 * clamp((nv:at01(x+40,y) - 0.4)*3, 0, 1) end},
         {deeprust, function(x,y) return LR(x,y) * (1 - B(x,y)) * 0.5 end}}
end

I'm noticing the bounce mask creates a hard edge that would show through a glaze, which isn't ideal. The critic wanted the rock's dark edge against the water to dissolve into shadow rather than stay sharp, so I need to merge those values at the boundary instead of leaving a visible outline.

The fix is a graded body-paint pass: rock color shifting toward water-dark/haze as it approaches the edge, with the weighting fading near the top of the mask so nothing hard-stops. I'll aim for a target edge value around 80, sitting between the rock's dark 56 and the water's 95, using a softened version of the bounce mask to control where this blend happens.

I'll shade the color within the piles rather than at the hard mask edge—keeping the top and inner edges matching the rock while lightening only the outer edge toward the water's value, simulating reflected light from the pool.

arguments.lua:
local nb = noise{seed=19101, period=60, octaves=2}
local function reach(x, y) return 26 + 14 * nb(x, y) + 20 * clamp((y - 1150)/80, 0, 1) end
local function w(x, y)
  local d = rE(math.min(math.max(y, 1110), 1250)) - x
  local t = clamp(1 - d / reach(x, y), 0, 1) ^ 1.3
  return t * clamp((y - 1132) / 34, 0, 1)
end
bounceM2 = fgRock3 * mask(function(x, y)
  if y < 1120 or y > 1256 or x < 170 then return 0 end
  local d = rE(math.min(y, 1250)) - x
  return (d >= -2 and d <= reach(x, y) + 10) and 1 or 0
end)
work(bounceM2, {hand="body", tool={kind="flat", width=7, stiffness=0.6}, length={14,34}, coverage=4, fill=true, clip=true, load=1.0,
  angle=function(x, y) return 1.35 + 0.1 * nb(x*2, y) end,
  piles={{rock, 1}, {lent, function(x,y) return 0.35 * (1 - w(x,y)) end},
         {waterdark, function(x,y) return 0.85 * w(x,y) end},
         {haze, function(x,y) return 0.32 * w(x,y) end},
         {amber, function(x,y) return 0.1 * w(x,y) end}}})
blend(bounceM2:shrink(2), {angle=1.35})

## End of sitting 4 (day 445) — handoff

State: everything dry. This sitting: at fresh eye I accepted both open passages. Then I took up the critic's campaign on the falls' outline: tapered dark wedges bite up into both outer edges from y~712 down, a few low-load fan threads veer out of the edges, and white tongues cross the shoulders of the foot rocks. The sheet now frays and widens as it falls, and the top 40–50 units under the lip stay crisp. I faded the thin ghost trunk into the haze with the background mix (body, load graded by height, blended). After the critic's fourth visit: broke the right-edge "rake" with one gap; re-shaped the foreground rock (flatter top to a corner, steep shadow side, moss as a wandering area that runs out at x~245, a soft warm lip toward the glow, two leaves); covered three of the even white glints on the dark left water with the water's own mix.

Accepted, with reasons (off the list):
- Stream above the brink: reads as the far water surface at full view; its faint plateau shows only at 2.4×. Repainted enough.
- Foam trails: read as foam drifting on the water at full view; lacy only up close.
- Ghost trunk (x~255): reads as a far trunk dissolving into the haze; a warming glaze turned it olive and was lifted.
- Foreground rock's right edge against the water: quiet at full view; a lighter "bounce" band read as a pasted panel and was lifted.
- Right foot rock's two small tongues and the left slot's V: read as water at full view.

Open passages: none

Practical lessons that still apply:
- Wet over DRY lifts clean with dipped rags (dip 1.0, pressure 1.0, width 10–24, 2–3 passes each way, fresh rags often). Trial on the painting is cheap; once a mark has dried it can only be covered, so check marks while they're open.
- To break a hard white edge: pointed "wedge" ribbons (top inside the sheet, widening down and out past the edge, roughen ~1.2/22) painted opaque with the neighbour's dark, clip, fill. Threads: fan 11, load .07–.15, pressure .3→.03, a few only, clipped to a band along the edge.
- Cover patches must match the substrate's value and texture: mix for the pool's dark water = waterdark .8 / haze .14 / amber .06; measure the mark's exact position with probe first.
- Glazes: gD2 over dry = gentle grayed step down; never blend a glaze over dry; a warm glaze over a cool gray mark goes olive.
- Small single gestures over big dark masses read as drawn lines; form comes from a few large graded planes (the foreground rock: one body pass with piles weighted by depth from the top contour, stroke angle turning from along-contour to vertical).
- clip=true for any pass bounded by a hard line; print mask:area() and look with mask= before painting; lose()'s where= must be a function or mask confined to the stretch you mean (a rect union gave rectangle outlines on scratch).
- Palette: 16 piles; scrape before knifing new ones; use lent for the black-umber dark.

Reflection: the falls became believable only when their silhouette stopped being a mask: the water frays where it is thinnest. The repeated lesson of this painting is that boundaries carry the reading: the waterline, the brink, the foam's bottom, the curtain's sides, the rock's moss band. Each read as fake while it was one even line, and each came alive when it was broken by the neighbour's own paint in tapered, unequal shapes. Next sitting: a look-only check of the whole canvas and a detail crop; if nothing new shows, the painting is finished.

content.text:
**Where the Light Comes Down (Autumn Falls)**: I painted on it this sitting, so it isn't formally finished yet. No passages are left open, and next sitting should be a look-only check.

It's a tall autumn woodland lit from behind. A gold glow deep in the trees, under an arch of rust and amber leaves, sends its light down onto a small four-strand waterfall over dark wet rock. White birches stand on the right bank, and the pool below holds a grayed gold reflection of the glow.

**What changed this sitting:**
- **Sides of the falls.** The critic pointed out that the curtain's outline was one hard white-on-black line, like a cut panel. I tested a fix on the scratch canvas first, then on the painting cut thin pointed dark gaps up into both outer edges and added a few faint white threads drifting outward. The sheet now frays and widens as it falls, the top stays smooth over the lip, and small white tongues spill over the shoulders of the rocks at its foot.
- **Foreground rock (lower left).** It was a smooth dome ringed by an even moss band, like a horseshoe. It now has a flatter top that turns at a corner into a steep side in shadow. The moss is a patch on the top that thins out toward the corner, with a soft warm edge facing the glow and two fallen leaves.
- **Smaller fixes.** The thin far trunk in the glow now fades into the haze instead of standing there as a stick. On the right edge of the falls, one gap breaks up a fan of evenly spaced threads that looked like a rake. Three even white ripple marks on the dark left water are now covered with the water's own colour.

**Tried and wiped off:** a lighter band along the foreground rock's water edge looked pasted on, and a warm glaze over the far trunk turned it olive. Both came off cleanly because the paint under them was dry.

**Accepted as they are:** the stream above the brink and the foam trails (they read well at viewing distance), the far trunk, the foreground rock's edge against the water, and the small tongues at the foot of the falls. My reasons are in the journal.

Open passages: none

**Practical lessons that still apply:**
- Wet paint laid over dry paint wipes off cleanly with a rag dipped in solvent, so trying something on the painting itself is cheap. Once a mark has dried it can only be painted over, so judge it while it is still wet.
- To break up a hard white edge, use tapered pointed gaps painted with the neighbouring dark, plus only a few faint threads.
- A cover patch has to match its surroundings in value and texture. For the pool's dark water the mix is `waterdark` .8, `haze` .14, `amber` .06. Find the mark's exact position with a probe first.
- Never blend a glaze over dry paint. A warm glaze over a cool gray mark turns olive.
- Form here comes from a few large graded planes. Small single marks over big dark masses read as drawn lines.
- Clip every pass that meets a hard edge, and check a mask's area and outline before painting through it.

The lesson this painting kept repeating is that its boundaries decide how it reads. The waterline, the brink, the foam, the sides of the falls and the moss band each looked false while it was one even line. Each came right once the neighbouring colour broke it into tapered, unequal shapes.
